setup.zh: 傍晚，石阶底下：舅舅在等你，镖师葛六也在。「进了门，头一件事，有人找你收钱。给不给，你自己掂量。」
setup.en: Dusk at the foot of the stair: your uncle is waiting, and so is the escort Ge Liu. "Once you're through the gate, first thing, someone comes to collect money. Pay or don't — weigh it yourself."

recap.zh: 开山门那天傍晚：舅舅在石阶底下等你；葛六说破了林子里那颗石子，又说「有人的地方，就有公中」。
recap.en: The evening the gate opened: your uncle waited at the foot of the stair; Ge Liu told you who paid for the pebble in the forest, and that "wherever there are people, there's a common fund".

en: At the foot of the stair, your uncle looks up.
"Wherever there are people, there's a common fund."

story.zh:
那天傍晚，新入门的弟子许到山门外头，跟送考的家里人说一句话，一炷香为限。小满从木架上取回了爷爷那张弓——第三排左数第七个，一个手指头也没人碰过——背在背上，跑下石阶。

头一级石阶上，坐着葛六，短刀横在膝盖上，腰里的钱袋瘪着。他看见小满，招了招手，道：「杂灵根，进了？」小满道：「进了。」葛六道：「林子里那颗石子，是马三一锭银子买的。我没接，他扣了我五两。」他站起身，把短刀插回腰里，「进了门，头一件事，有人找你收钱。有人的地方，就有公中。给不给，你自己掂量——你这样的，掂量得清。」说完，他顺着泗水往北走了，走镖去了。小满站在那里，把这两句话在心里各记了一笔。

舅舅站在不远处，仰着脸，也不知站了多久，青布长衫的下摆全是泥。他一看见小满，先不问考上没考上，先问：「饿不饿？」小满道：「饿。」舅舅从怀里摸出一个炊饼——早上在山门底下买的，他自己没舍得吃——塞进他手里，这才问：「……考上了？」小满道：「外门。」

舅舅一把抓住了他的胳膊，抓得死紧。他转过身，对着旁边一个不认识的老头，大声道：「我外甥！考上了！三百级，一口气！」那老头吓了一跳。舅舅又对着另一个不认识的妇人道：「我外甥！」那妇人也吓了一跳。

马家的滑竿也停在石阶底下，马小宝换了一条干裤子，坐在上头，也是出来跟他爹说一句话的。马三的脸色已经缓过来了，瞧见舅舅，笑了一声：「杂灵根，下下之资，还是观主开恩添的一个。沈家的，别高兴得太早——下下之资，熬不到腊月那五两银子，就得卷铺盖下山。」舅舅这一路上，见了马三从来不抬头，这时候却抬起头来，道：「熬得到。我外甥是他自己两条腿走上去的；你家那一位，是四个轿夫抬上去的。」马三的脸一沉，要说什么，滑竿上的马小宝已经嚷着饿了。他瞪了舅舅一眼，把一包桂花糕塞给儿子，带着家丁下山去了。舅舅望着他的背影，腰杆挺了一挺，又道：「当年，我也爬到了一百八十级——」小满道：「舅舅。」舅舅道：「……一百六十级。」

小满道：「舅舅，一百六十级那里，崖壁上刻满了字，都是在那一级上坐下过的人刻的。」舅舅不说话了。他把脸转过去，朝着泗水那边，看了很久。小满道：「舅舅，我替你走上来了。」舅舅没有回头。过了好一会儿，他才开口，声音有点哑，道：「……风大。」他拿袖子在脸上抹了一把，又抹了一把，然后转回来，把小满背上那张弓扶正了，把他的衣领翻好——翻衣领的那一下，同他姐姐一模一样——道：「回去吧。一炷香到了。」

小满走上石阶，走到第十级，回头看，舅舅还站在那儿。走到第五十级，回头看，舅舅还站在那儿。走到一百级，雾起来了，再回头，就看不见了。

那天夜里，牛棚里那个兖州来的孩子，蜷在草铺上，脸朝着墙。他爹坐在他旁边，一口一口地抽着旱烟，抽完一锅，又装一锅。舅舅挪过去，挨着那个爹坐下了。他没提自己的外甥，只道：「我当年，也没上去。爬到一百六十级，腿就动不了了。下了山，去县里学打算盘，如今在济世堂做账房，娶了媳妇，生了个闺女。」他顿了一顿，又道：「挺好的。」蜷在墙角的那个孩子，肩膀动了一下。后来兖州那个爹问他：「老哥，你当年，到底爬到了多少级？」舅舅想了一想，道：「一百六十级。」那是他这辈子，头一回，没有多说十级。
story.en:
Toward evening that day the new disciples were allowed out of the gate to say a word to the family who'd brought them, for the length of one stick of incense. Xiaoman took his grandfather's bow back from the rack — third row, seventh from the left, not a finger laid on it — slung it on his back, and ran down the stair.

On the bottom step sat Ge Liu, his short knife across his knees, his purse flat at his waist. He saw Xiaoman and beckoned. "Mixed root. In?" Xiaoman said, "In." Ge Liu said: "That pebble in the forest — Ma San bought it with a silver ingot. I didn't take it, so he docked me five taels." He stood and slid the knife back into his belt. "Once you're through the gate, first thing, someone comes to collect money. Wherever there are people, there's a common fund. Pay or don't — weigh it yourself. Your sort can weigh it." And with that he walked off north along the Si, back to guarding caravans. Xiaoman stood there and put each of the two sentences down on his books.

His uncle stood not far off, face turned up; how long he'd been standing there no one knew, the hem of his blue cotton gown all mud. The moment he saw Xiaoman, before asking whether he'd passed, he asked: "Hungry?" Xiaoman said, "Hungry." His uncle took a griddle cake from his coat — bought at the gate that morning, and he hadn't had the heart to eat it himself — pressed it into his hand, and only then asked: "…Got in?" Xiaoman said, "Outer court."

His uncle seized his arm and gripped it tight. He turned to an old man he didn't know and said loudly: "My nephew! Got in! Three hundred steps, one go!" The old man jumped. His uncle turned to a woman he didn't know: "My nephew!" The woman jumped too.

The Ma sedan chair was stopped at the foot of the stair too, Ma Xiaobao on it in a dry pair of trousers, come out to say his word to his father as well. Ma San's colour had come back; he saw the uncle and laughed. "A mixed root, lowest of the low, and only the one the abbot added out of kindness. Don't celebrate too soon, Shens — the lowest of the low won't last till the five taels come in the twelfth month; he'll be rolling up his bedding and walking down." All along the road his uncle had never once looked up at Ma San; now he looked up. "He'll last. My nephew walked up there on his own two legs; yours, four bearers carried up." Ma San's face darkened; he was about to say something, but Ma Xiaobao on the chair was already whining that he was hungry. Ma San glared at the uncle, thrust a packet of osmanthus cakes at his son, and went off down the mountain with his servants. His uncle watched his back and straightened a little, and said again: "Back then, I climbed to step one hundred and eighty myself —" Xiaoman said, "Uncle." His uncle said: "…One hundred and sixty."

Xiaoman said, "Uncle, at step one hundred and sixty the cliff wall is covered in writing — all carved by people who sat down on that step." His uncle fell silent. He turned his face toward the Si and looked a long time. Xiaoman said, "Uncle, I walked up for you." His uncle didn't turn round. After a good while he spoke, his voice a little hoarse: "…Windy." He wiped his face with his sleeve, and wiped it again; then turned back, set the bow straight on Xiaoman's back, turned his collar straight — that turn of the collar exactly like his sister's — and said: "Go on back. The incense is out."

Xiaoman went up the stair. At the tenth step he looked back; his uncle was still standing there. At the fiftieth step he looked back; his uncle was still standing there. At the hundredth the mist rose, and when he looked back he couldn't see him.

That night in the cowshed the Yanzhou boy lay curled on the straw, face to the wall. His father sat beside him smoking a long pipe, bowl after bowl. His uncle moved over and sat down beside that father. He didn't mention his nephew; he said only: "I didn't get up either, back then. Got to step one hundred and sixty, and my legs wouldn't move. Came down, went to the county to learn the abacus; now I keep the books at the Jishi Hall, took a wife, had a daughter." He paused. "It's all right." The boy curled in the corner, his shoulders moved. Later the Yanzhou father asked him: "Old brother, how many steps did you really climb, back then?" His uncle thought a moment. "One hundred and sixty." It was the first time in his life he hadn't added ten.

exits.means: pays the one stone to the common fund, keeps the peace for now

refuse.en: You have no spirit stones on you.

what.zh: 外门的「公中」：收了你一块灵石。
what.en: The outer court's "common fund": took one of your spirit stones.

story.zh:
小满把葛六那两句话，在心里掂量了一路。他掂量出来的是：一块灵石，买一个「懂事」，买马小宝一个月不来找麻烦。这笔账，眼下划得来。

第二天一早，饭堂门口，他从怀里摸出一块灵石，交了。马小宝掂了一掂，冲他笑，笑得跟他爹一模一样。

他心里却记了一笔：公中，一块。马小宝。
story.en:
Xiaoman weighed Ge Liu's two sentences all the way up the stair. What he weighed out was: one spirit stone buys "knowing his place", buys a month of Ma Xiaobao leaving him alone. For now, the sum comes out in his favour.

Next morning at the refectory door he took a spirit stone from his jacket and handed it over. Ma Xiaobao weighed it in his palm and grinned at him, a grin exactly like his father's.

But in his heart he entered a line: Common fund, one stone. Ma Xiaobao.

exits.means: refuses to pay the common fund

story.zh:
小满把葛六那两句话，在心里掂量了一路，掂量出来一个字：不。他把怀里的灵石一块一块放进他娘给的那个空钱袋里，叮，叮，叮。空钱袋里，头一回有了东西。

他知道往后会怎样：马小宝不会当着人的面动手，他会等。他爹就是这么收租的——先笑，再等，等你以为没事了，门就飞了。那就等。
story.en:
Xiaoman weighed Ge Liu's two sentences all the way up the stair, and weighed out one word: no. He put the spirit stones from his jacket one by one into the empty purse his mother had given him — *ting, ting, ting*. For the first time, the empty purse held something.

He knew what would come of it: Ma Xiaobao wouldn't lift a hand in front of people; he'd wait. That was how his father collected rent — grin first, then wait, wait till you think it's over, and then the door flies. Then let him wait.
